explanation: Fires in code and markup on the token right before or at the start of an identifier or string literal argument, e.g. the opening quote after require( / from / import, or a quoted string-start like ' or " ; also weaker on mid-identifier pieces in code (operator.attrgetter, StringEscapeUtils, iso-8859). Prose tokens barely fire.

Fires on a subword piece that starts with or is 's'/'os' joining two word parts inside a compound word, especially Greek/Latin scientific compounds (psych-os-ocial, olig-os-accharide, fluor-os-copy, somat-os-ensory) and hyphen/slash-s joins (free-spirited, work/life/school, cyberspace). Strongest on the 'os'/'s' connector token mid-word; weaker on other mid-word pieces like 'ores' in electrophoresis.

Mixed: mid-word subword pieces in names and rare words (Re-he-aring, THEM-SEL-VES, Share-A-like, Gay-ath-ri), legal-document headers ('Motion for Rehearing'), and the preposition 'at' in technical 'at right angles / at a position' phrases, plus words like 'your' in license text. No single shared trigger.

Fires on a word that completes a short fixed phrase or heading, typically a noun right after a capitalized word or determiner in titles/section headers (Bi-ography heading in Wikipedia bios, Folk-lore, 'Your success', 'The Solution', 'The Hill'), and on phrase-completing tokens like 'if all else', 'fire broke out'. Strongest for the 'Biography'/section-header completion; otherwise diffuse.

Fires on interior subword pieces of technical/scientific terms, especially chemistry and analytical methods (mass spectrom-etry, fluoro-quin-olone, R-aman, casp-ase, proteog-ly-cans, perov-sk-ite) and digits inside technical identifiers (STM32, CV_32FC3, 99mTc). Ordinary prose words fire weakly.

Fires on content or function words in the middle of informal or argumentative English prose, often the word that completes a common idiomatic phrase (a copy 'of', be 'there', the right 'thing', bring you 'back', sorted 'out', what he said he 'would'). Very diffuse with no clear token or context restriction.

Fires on subword tokens inside South Asian (mostly Indian) personal and place names, e.g. Ansh-ul, Pram-od, Pran-av, Ar-un, Minak-sh-isundaram, Kanyakumari, and also on the year digit in contexts about Modi/India. Strongest mid-name; non-Indian contexts barely fire.

Fires on a noun or pronoun completing a common technical/formal collocation (genetic diversity, nutritional status, PRIMARY KEY, microcomputer system, wireless data communication, C#, its publication), plus scattered code tokens. Diffuse with no single trigger.

Strongly fires on the word 'already' and on the quantifier 'some' (as in 'some are', 'just some poses'), and also on 'enough', 'actual'; additional unrelated hits on nouns inside named terms (Science Citation Index, Longleaf Drive, Apo-B) and code tokens. Core is 'already'/'some' quantity-time adverbs; the rest is noise.

Fires most strongly on the word 'mobile' as a modifier (mobile device, mobile telephone, mobile-first), and also on other prenominal modifiers that start a compound (mid-1970s, rebel-controlled, multiple cores, DNA methylation, non-smoker, Marvel). Mainly 'mobile', with offshoots to other compound modifiers.

Fires on whitespace, punctuation and identifier fragments in code snippets embedded in Q&A posts (indentation before 'private', space before version number, newline after import, ')' before .then), plus scattered prose/LaTeX tokens. No coherent meaning beyond 'formatting tokens in code'.

Fires on subword pieces in non-English or rare words (ALBU-QU-ERQUE, Lem-ait-re, den-ials, Kitsch-vor-wurfs, Italian/French/Spanish text) and on compiler flag letters (-f in gcc flags). Generally word-interior fragments in unusual words; diffuse.

Fires on evaluative adjectives/adverbs describing ease, difficulty, quality or comfort, especially after 'how' or 'as' or in 'a ___' (how difficult, how painful, how lucky, as smooth as possible, easy and secure, tough, comfortable, clean, sleek, sharpness). Neutral descriptive adjectives fire weakly.

Fires on the final or interior subword piece of a multi-token word or name (two-hit, p53's '3', FLOT-US, meditat-ion, RELIG-ION, Roose-velt, Ri-ordan, PI3-K), across biomedical, legal and multilingual text. Essentially word-completion pieces with no topical restriction.

Fires on existential 'there' (There is/are/was/exists/'s), especially at sentence or clause start after a period, comma or 'so/and/if'. Locative 'there'/'here' and 'thereupon' fire moderately; other tokens barely fire.

Fires on function words and contraction pieces in mixed text and code ('t in doesn't/didn't, 'and', 'or', 'of', 'for', 'first', closing quote in exception names, Portuguese verbs). No common semantic or syntactic trigger evident.

Fires on assorted tokens: long whitespace runs in legal document headers, the '/' in scores like 8/10, list/sequence pieces in math, and diverse function words in prose (is, other, for, that, of). No coherent pattern.

Fires partly on sentence-initial discourse words starting a new sentence after a period, especially 'In' (also '.In' with no space, 'For', 'This'), and partly on assorted mid-word or code tokens (KEYPOINT, data volume, Prion, recombination). Two loosely related jobs at best.

Fires on the token completing a fixed formulaic phrase: 'Apache License' in license headers, 'state of' in 'in the U.S. state of', 'Memorandum Opinion', and on final subword pieces of drug/biomedical terms (rivarox-aban, plasmin-ogen, erythropo-iet-in, cut-aneous). Mostly completion of predictable multi-token terms.

Fires on a token that begins or continues a technical compound/keyword after a fixed preceding word, e.g. 'gram' in gram-negative, 'INTO' after INSERT, comment markers '//' and '<!--' at line start in code, 'TRIGGER', 'season' after ordinal. Mixed between code keywords/comment starts and technical terms in prose.

Fires on subword pieces containing 'ne'/'ine'/'te' within words or names (calc-ine-urin, sensor-ine-ural, ne-urokinin, Ne-dlands, NE-VADA, Ne-ves, ne-komata, Entre-prene-urs, Tea Party, Pod-casts). Largely orthographic 'n/e' fragments mid-word.
